content: Candida is a normal commensal organism found on the skin and mucous membranes. Its pathogenicity is typically kept in check by a healthy immune system and intact, regenerating skin. However, under certain conditions, Candida can become virulent and cause infection. Pathogenesis and Virulence Factors: 1. Adherence Molecules: Candida secretes molecules that facilitate its adherence to host cells, enabling colonization and infection. 2. Hydrolase Production: The fungus produces hydrolases, which have a lytic effect on tissues, aiding in its invasion and spread. 3. Polymorphism: Candida can grow in two forms—pseudohyphae (elongated ellipsoid forms) and yeast (rounded or oval budding forms). While the exact role of polymorphism in virulence is unclear, species capable of severe disease often exhibit this ability. 4. Biofilm Formation: Candida can form thick biofilms on mucosal surfaces, catheters, and dentures. Biofilms provide a protective environment for the fungus, making it more resistant to treatment. Conditions that compromise cell-mediated immunity, worsen the patient’s general health, or create a favorable medium for biofilm formation increase the risk of candidiasis. 5. Gene VPS4: This gene plays a significant role in oropharyngeal candidiasis. Mutations in this gene are associated with reduced virulence. Gross Pathology: Oropharyngeal candidiasis can present in four distinct forms: 1. Pseudomembranous Candidiasis: Characterized by curdy white discharge visible on examination. It is commonly seen in newborns or immunocompromised patients, such as those on corticosteroids. 2. Atrophic Candidiasis: Presents as erythema or edema without the characteristic white plaques. It is often associated with dental dentures. 3. Chronic Hyperplastic Candidiasis (Candidal Leukoplakia): Persistent, tough, adherent white lesions that require biopsy for differentiation from other leukoplakias. It is more common in smokers and patients with iron deficiency anemia or impaired cell-mediated immunity. 4. Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis (CMCC): A syndrome involving chronic or recurrent superficial Candida infections of the skin and mucous membranes, often associated with endocrine and autoimmune disorders. It is characterized by T-cell dysfunction in response to Candida antigens. Patients may present with recurrent or chronic infections, which are usually superficial but can become invasive, particularly in newborns. Endocrinopathies such as hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency may accompany CMCC. Microscopic Pathology: Wet mount examination with 10% KOH or saline reveals hyphae, pseudohyphae, and blastospores. Histopathological examination shows blastospores and pseudohyphae in the superficial epithelial layer, which is characteristic of candidiasis. However, blastospores can also be seen in other opportunistic fungal infections like Cryptococcus neoformans or Histoplasma capsulatum, especially in immunocompromised patients. If only blastospores are evident, further smear examination for pseudohyphae is recommended. Subtypes of Candidiasis: 1. Pseudomembranous Candidiasis: The epithelium appears thickened with parakeratosis (superficial separation of the epithelial layer). Polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs) infiltrate the epithelium, and chronic inflammatory cells infiltrate the lamina propria. Pseudohyphae are embedded within the epithelium. 2. Atrophic Candidiasis: Similar to pseudomembranous candidiasis but lacks parakeratosis. The epithelium is atrophic and thin. 3. Hyperplastic Candidiasis: The epithelium is hyperplastic, hyperkeratotic, and acanthotic, with dysplasia in some cases. Clinical Presentation: Oropharyngeal candidiasis can manifest in various ways: Many cases are asymptomatic, particularly in mild disease or patients with poor general health. Symptoms may include dysphagia, odynophagia, white patches on the mouth and tongue (in pseudomembranous subtype), difficulty tasting food, and a sensation of fullness or discomfort in the mouth. Thrush and Breastfeeding: The increased use of antibiotics in laboring women to prevent Group B streptococcal transmission has led to a rise in thrush cases. Symptoms include: Oral rash in the infant’s mouth. Diaper rash resistant to conventional treatments. Burning, painful nipples in breastfeeding mothers, which can range from mild to severe and complicate breastfeeding. Over-the-counter yeast infection creams (7-day packages) can be applied to the skin with improvement seen within 24–48 hours. Creams should be washed off nipples before breastfeeding. Physical Examination: The appearance of the skin and mucous membranes varies by subtype: 1. Pseudomembranous Oropharyngeal Candidiasis: White plaques on the mouth and tongue. Attempting to remove the patches with a tongue depressor leaves an erythematous area, sometimes with bleeding, distinguishing it from lichen planus. 2. Atrophic Oropharyngeal Candidiasis: Also known as denture stomatitis. Lesions appear as erythematous areas without white plaques, typically at the contact sites of dental dentures. 3. Hyperplastic Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (Candidal Leukoplakia): Plaques are rough, irregular, and nodular on an erythematous base, often found on both sides of the buccal mucosa and less frequently on the tongue. Non-homogeneous (speckled) leukoplakias are common. 4. Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis: Recurrent or persistent Candida infections in the mouth, tongue, scalp, and nails. Chronicity often leads to disfigurement and thickening of affected areas. Nails appear brittle and broken. Rarely, the condition may progress to systemic candidiasis, especially in the presence of another immunodeficiency. Autoimmune disorders such as hypoparathyroidism, diabetes mellitus, or Graves’ disease are frequently associated. Laboratory Findings: Diagnosis of oropharyngeal candidiasis is primarily clinical, with confirmatory diagnostic tests rarely needed. Oral smears are obtained by gently scraping lesions and spreading the debris on a glass slide. In hyperplastic candidiasis, biopsy is indicated. Both smears and biopsies can be stained using periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which stains fungal walls red, or Gram stain, where Candida appears strongly Gram-positive. Histopathological Examination: Blastospores (yeast form) and pseudohyphae in the superficial epithelial layer are characteristic of candidiasis. However, blastospores may also be present in other opportunistic fungal infections, necessitating further examination for pseudohyphae if Candida is clinically suspected. In pseudomembranous candidiasis, the epithelium is thickened with parakeratosis, infiltrated by PMNs, and shows chronic inflammatory cells in the lamina propria. Pseudohyphae appear as weakly basophilic structures embedded within the epithelium. Atrophic candidiasis lacks parakeratosis, with the epithelium appearing atrophic and thin. Hyperplastic candidiasis shows hyperplastic, hyperkeratotic, and acanthotic epithelium, with dysplasia in some cases. Causes: The most common cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis is Candida albicans.
